title: Menno Mart thrift store approved; proceeds to go to Steinbach Community Outreach
summary: Menno Mart, a non-profit building-materials resale store, asked for a conditional use to open at 62 Life Sciences Parkway (M1 zone). Its presenter said profits would go to local charities, including Steinbach Community Outreach. Council approved without objection; Steinbach Community Outreach itself was not discussed.
status_detail: Conditional use CU-2016-01 approved the same night. This is the only time Steinbach Community Outreach is named at council in Dec 2015 – 2020 apart from a passing reference by a Headway presenter (Apr 5, 2016).
figures: Store expected to employ 2–4 people (transcript 1:09:22).
public: B.S. (Menno Mart) presented; no objectors.
notes: Included as context only: the decision was a land-use approval, not a homelessness measure. Mover heard as 'Councilor Siemens. Motion to approve' (1:12:16); seconder not reliably heard.

title: Meth and addiction raised mainly through RCMP reports
summary: Addiction came up mostly in RCMP quarterly reports. In 2016 the staff sergeant said Steinbach had 'a meth issue' driving petty theft. In 2018 Councillor Earl Funk asked how meth was affecting the city, and the RCMP linked it to vehicle theft, mischief and shoplifting. In 2019 Mayor Funk thanked the RCMP for 'working on our meth crisis'. In 2020 Councillor Jake Hiebert spoke about addiction and mental health in an opening. Council kept 'drug use reduction' and organized crime among its annual RCMP priorities. Treatment or housing was not discussed.
status_detail: Council confirmed RCMP priorities (organized crime, property crime, visibility, traffic) each year; no city action on addiction treatment, outreach or housing was proposed in 2015–2020.
figures: Meth 'about $10 to be high for a day' (RCMP, 2018-05-15 0:09:42).
reasons: enforcement-first: Raised meth as a question for the RCMP and later credited the RCMP with work on the 'meth crisis'. (Earl Funk)
public: RCMP Staff Sergeant H.L. (RCMP detachment commander, presenting to council) linked meth to petty crime in 2016 and 2018.
notes: Not homelessness directly; included because addiction is how the issue surfaced. A 2016 Mental Health Act amendment welcomed by a Councillor Penner (2016-07-05, which Penner is unclear) is left out as policing/health-system context. The 2020 opening's personal content is not quoted or described (report sensitivity rule).

title: Opening remarks credit churches and charities for helping 'the less fortunate'
summary: In his opening remarks, Councillor John Fehr described Steinbach as a benevolent city and credited churches and charities, naming Today House, Soups On, Helping Hands, Agape House and others, for the social, practical and spiritual help they give people in need.
status_detail: Remarks only; no motion or follow-up. It states the period's prevailing view that help for people in need comes from churches and charities.
reasons: partners-do-it: Churches and charities 'minister outside of their walls' to help the less fortunate. (John Fehr)

title: Variance to add one-bedroom suites for Eden Health clients denied over parking
summary: DeWalt Custom Homes asked to build 22 suites instead of 15 at 295 Loewen Boulevard with 26 parking stalls instead of the 36 required, because Eden Health (a Mennonite program serving people with mental illness) wanted to rent one-bedroom suites for its clients. The applicant said Eden had 40 applicants it could not house, only 8 of whom needed parking. Staff recommended denial. Neighbours objected over parking and property values. Council denied the variance on parking grounds.
status_detail: Variance V-2016-20 denied. Councillor Siemens acknowledged 'an ongoing need' but cited parking and no written long-term commitment from Eden. Eden's need for one-bedroom suites came back at its Nov 2017 delegation.
figures: 22 suites with 26 stalls proposed vs 36 stalls required by Zoning By-law 2055 (staff, 0:08:09); Eden had 40 applications it could not place, 8 needing parking (applicant, 0:11:00); by-law requires 1.5 stalls per unit plus 10% visitor parking (Zwaagstra, 0:22:06).
reasons: wrong-location: The parking minimum exists for the long term; future tenants might need more stalls, and this is a busy street. (Michael Zwaagstra); wrong-location: Too much street parking near apartment blocks; 1.5 stalls is a minimum; no written long-term commitment from Eden. (Jac Siemens); wrong-location: Administration found the request not compatible with the surrounding neighbourhood and recommended denial. (Troy Warkentin (City Manager))
public: Neighbouring owners (initials withheld) objected over parking, safety and difficulty selling their house. The applicant, L.S., relayed Eden Health's need for suites.
vote: carried (motion to deny), no opposition heard
notes: Diarization splits Siemens's reply across labels C and I. The two Councillor Penners asked questions (0:12:36, 0:13:13) but could not be told apart.

title: Eden Foundation briefs council on supportive housing and the singles waitlist
summary: At council's invitation, Eden Foundation and Eden Health Care Services described their Steinbach programs: 48 subsidized or affordable suites (Penfield and Wilson Courts), a weekday mental-health drop-in, and help finding housing. The longest waitlist was for single people needing one-bedroom suites, whom Manitoba Housing did not serve. A planned building proposal was on hold. Mayor Goertzen asked about gaps and long-term plans; Councillor Siemens asked how Eden avoids overlap with Today House, Agape House and Helping Hands.
status_detail: Information only; Eden made no request and council took no action. The city gave Eden Foundation a $200 grant for 2017 (R18-065).
figures: 24 suites at Penfield, 24 at Wilson Courts; about 30 regular drop-in attenders; 6–10 open housing-search files at a time (B.D., 0:17:46).
reasons: partners-do-it: Concerned about overlap among the many community organizations doing similar work. (Jac Siemens)
public: B.D. (Eden Housing and Supports Program) said single adults under 55 were the hardest to house and a building proposal was on the back burner.
notes: The Eden Foundation speaker who introduced B.D. ('Mr. Corman', 'Gerry' as heard) is not quoted.

title: Agape House (women's shelter) proclamation requests received as information
summary: Agape House, the area's domestic-violence shelter, asked council each December to proclaim or support its Dec 6 event (National Day of Remembrance and Action on Violence Against Women). In 2017 Mayor Goertzen looked for a councillor to attend the event. In 2018 Mayor Funk said council would be at a meeting with the RM of Hanover and took the request as information. In 2019 the request was acknowledged in the minutes.
status_detail: No proclamation resolution appears in the 2018 or 2019 minutes (2018-12-04 item 29, 2019-11-19 item 18: 'acknowledged'). Agape House is not on the 2017–2019 city grant lists.
public: Agape House (organization) wrote to council.
notes: No transcript exists for Nov 19, 2019; that item is from the minutes only. Agape House is a domestic-violence shelter, not a general homeless shelter; it is included because it is the only shelter organization in the record.

title: Councillor Fehr describes a homeless man who lived behind his shop
summary: Councillor John Fehr opened the meeting with an account of a man he had found sleeping behind his business, who told him he had lived in the yard for five days the previous October without anyone noticing. Fehr called him 'one of many homeless people in this community' and said he felt helpless to do more than offer coffee and toast.
status_detail: The first time a council member said on the record that Steinbach has many homeless people. No discussion, motion or follow-up came from it in 2018–2020.

title: Token city grants to Eden Foundation ($200) and Today House ($300) for 2017, none after
summary: Council's annual grants list for 2017 included $200 for Eden Foundation and $300 for Today House, out of $887,371.78 in grants. Neither appears on the 2018 or 2019 lists.
status_detail: R18-065 accepted the 2017 grants unanimously. The 2018 list (R19-073, $1,559,883.21) and the 2019 list (R20-064, $932,853.54) have no grants to Eden, Today House, Agape House or Steinbach Community Outreach.
figures: 2017: Eden Foundation $200, Today House $300 of $887,371.78 (minutes R18-065). 2018: total $1,559,883.21 incl. Bethesda Foundation $500,000 and HSD Headway Fund $8,000 (R19-073). 2019: total $932,853.54 (R20-064).
notes: Grants lists were not debated on the record. Lists for 2015 and 2016 are not available (no minutes).

title: Residents raise homelessness and 'vulnerable people' at housing hearings
summary: At three general housing hearings residents raised homelessness or low-income need. At the 2018 Official Community Plan hearing, T.B. asked whether the plan addressed the need of seniors, homeless people and low-income families. At a 2019 rezoning for a 9-unit building, A.D. welcomed bachelor and one-bedroom units for homeless and young people. At a 2020 rezoning, C.S. said Steinbach has many vulnerable people who cannot afford $1,000 rents. Council did not discuss homelessness in reply; it approved both rezonings (Zwaagstra moved, Siemens seconded).
status_detail: No answer on homelessness was recorded. Administration said the 2018 plan changes affected mainly annexed land. By-law 2120 got second reading unanimously on May 21, 2019 (R19-118; third reading July 2, 2019), and By-law 2148 got second and third readings unanimously on June 16, 2020 (R20-127, R20-128), as general housing decisions.
figures: Rents of '$1,000 a month' in new First Street units (C.S., 2020-06-16 0:20:28).
public: T.B. (2018), A.D. (2019) and C.S. (2020), residents. Objectors at the 2019 hearing called prospective renters 'riffraff'.
notes: These were general housing hearings (covered by the housing report); included only for the homelessness mentions. No 2018-07-17 minutes are available.

title: Today House asks for one-time funding for essential repairs; received as information
summary: Today House wrote asking for one-time, project-specific funding for essential repairs. Two weeks after the new council took office, the request was taken as information without discussion.
status_detail: Minutes: 'Correspondence was acknowledged from Today House with a request of a one-time funding to cover project - specific funding for essential repairs.' No grant to Today House appears on the 2018 (R19-073) or 2019 (R20-064) grants lists.
figures: Amount not stated in the minutes or transcript.
public: Today House (organization) wrote to council.
notes: Which councillor said 'Take his information' (Speaker C, 0:21:12) is not identified. Today House's 2018 role is not described in the record; by 2026 it was described as Steinbach Community Outreach's small referral-based shelter (existing report), which is not verified for 2018.

title: Council picks Steinbach Community Outreach for the $1.34M provincial affordable-housing grant
summary: The province gave Steinbach a $1,337,500 conditional grant (announced March 2021) to place with an affordable-housing project. Three proposals came in (Vogt Building 18 units, Habitat for Humanity duplex, Steinbach Community Outreach 24 units). Administration recommended forwarding both Habitat and SCO; council forwarded only SCO so the whole grant went to one project, citing SCO's work with homeless and low-income people.
status_detail: MHRC recommended approval (letter Dec 9, 2021, per Adam Thiessen on Jul 5, 2022); council formally awarded the grant Jul 5, 2022 (R22-161). The project became The Bridge (24 units at 224 Woodhaven Ave).
figures: Grant $1,337,500 (Thiessen, Jul 5 2022 0:05:15; "$1.337 million", Zwaagstra Nov 2 2021 0:09:32); 24 units, originally at 330 Stonebridge Crossing (Thiessen 0:07:01); SCO had raised $350,000 and pledged over $700,000 (Mayor Funk 0:14:42).
public: No public speakers. A letter from Bridge Park Manor supported the original Stonebridge Crossing site (Zwaagstra, Siemens).
notes: No speaker map for 2021; speakers identified from chair hand-offs and the minutes.

title: Parking variance for The Bridge approved against staff advice
summary: SCO moved its 24-unit project to 224 Woodhaven Ave after Bridge Park Manor withdrew support for the first site, and asked to build 30 parking stalls instead of the required 40. Administration recommended denial because of traffic on Woodhaven; council approved the variance unanimously, accepting SCO's evidence that very low-income tenants rarely own cars.
status_detail: Approved subject to bachelor/1-bedroom suites only, a grant funding agreement before a permit, and a development agreement (friendly amendment by Zwaagstra).
figures: 30 stalls vs 40 required (Warkentin 0:13:37); rents $583 bachelor / $801 one-bedroom incl. utilities, income caps $23,500 / $32,000 (Siemens 0:51:59; SCO delegation); SCO serving 765 individuals a year (I.K. 0:17:05); donation pledges over $850,000 (SCO building committee, 0:27:49).
public: I.K. (SCO executive director) and SCO building-committee members R.P. and C.K. presented: 14 prospective tenants, only 4 with vehicles; comparable Eden East buildings use 7 and 15 stalls of 24. Neighbour N.P. raised general concerns about privacy, litter and theft behind Whitby Crescent but did not oppose.
notes: Transcript says "224 Reimer Avenue" at 0:13:37; minutes and other turns say 224 Woodhaven Avenue.

title: $1,337,500 grant to SCO approved, secured by a 20-year forgivable mortgage (By-law 2210)
summary: After MHRC approval, council formally awarded the provincial grant to SCO and passed By-law 2210, lending the grant as an interest-free second mortgage forgiven over 20 years so the units stay affordable. No city money was involved.
status_detail: R22-161 (grant) and R22-163 (By-law 2210 first and second readings) Jul 5, 2022; R22-185 third reading Aug 2, 2022. The Bridge opened in 2023 (per the existing report; opening not discussed at a recorded meeting).
figures: $1,337,500 (Thiessen 0:05:15); estimated project cost $3.6M in Nov 2021 (Siemens 0:06:23); 12 bachelor suites of 400 sq ft and 12 one-bedroom of 600 sq ft (Siemens 0:06:23); mortgage reduced 1/20 per year, no interest (Siemens 0:12:24).
seconder: Michael Zwaagstra (R22-161); Susan Penner (R22-163); Jake Hiebert (R22-185)

title: SCO's $65,000 funding request for The Bridge received as information
summary: Steinbach Community Outreach wrote asking for a $65,000 grant for The Bridge. Council took it as information with no discussion or funding motion.
status_detail: Received as information (minutes item 17). No later city grant to SCO found in the minutes or transcripts.
public: Steinbach Community Outreach (letter).
notes: The package for Nov 15, 2022 is not on file, so the purpose of the $65,000 is not known beyond "The Bridge".

title: Councillor Jake Hiebert's opening on homelessness in Steinbach
summary: In his meeting opening, Councillor Jake Hiebert, a former police officer, described people he meets living in tents behind churches and businesses in Steinbach and asked whether society is "enabling" homelessness or should focus on mental health, shelters and unemployment, which he said need government to act.
status_detail: Opening remarks only; no motion.
reasons: attracts-people: asked whether services that feed and supply homeless people enable "this culture to grow" (Jake Hiebert); provincial-responsibility: long-term answers need trained professionals and "a willingness of government" (Jake Hiebert)

title: City joins the provincial Community Safety and Well-Being plan (staff time only); plan released 2026
summary: The province funded a Community Safety and Well-Being (CSWB) plan for 12 communities, run by the Canadian Centre for Safer Communities with Headway. Council agreed to take part with up to 2 staff hours a week, stressing the city is only a "conduit" and no city tax dollars are involved. The finished plan was released in March 2026 and received as information.
status_detail: Plan finalized and posted Mar 3, 2026 (received as information). The province funds $60,000 for plan priorities, distributed by the CSWB steering committee (Thiessen, Jul 21, 2026). Per the existing report, the plan's housing goals include creating shelter space/emergency housing in Steinbach; no council action on that goal found by Nov 2026.
figures: Province $1.3M for 12 communities (Zwaagstra 0:12:01); $60,000 per community (Thiessen 0:08:52); staff time not over 2 hrs/week (Thiessen 0:08:52); 872 survey responses (Mayor Funk, Mar 3 2026, 0:20:43).
reasons: partners-do-it: city's role is a conduit between the province and social service providers (Adam Thiessen); already-doing-enough: plan "really just summarizes what's already happening" in local organizations (Earl Funk)
notes: Plan content (shelter goal, coordinator) is from the published plan as cited in answers/homelessness; not re-read here.

title: Southeast Helping Hands' $245,000 grant request received as information
summary: Southeast Helping Hands (food bank) asked the city for $245,000. Council took it as information without discussion.
status_detail: Received as information (minutes item 14); no funding motion found later.
public: Southeast Helping Hands (letter).
notes: Purpose of the $245,000 not stated in the minutes or transcript (Feb 6, 2024 package not on file). Helping Hands is a food bank, so this is adjacent to homelessness rather than a housing request.

title: Agape House (domestic-violence shelter) requests received as information
summary: Agape House asked for sponsorship of an International Women's Day event (Feb 2024) and for participation in its Ribbons of Hope campaign (Nov 2025); both were received as information.
status_detail: Received as information both times (minutes Feb 20, 2024 item 24; Nov 4, 2025 item 18).
public: Agape House (letters).
notes: Minor; Agape House is listed in SCOPE. Neither request concerned shelter capacity.

title: Secondary-suite safety enforcement: Siemens warns it could add to homelessness
summary: Council backed administration's plan to enforce the 2021 secondary-suite safety by-law (2157), including fines up to $1,000 a day and decommissioning suites that cannot comply. Councillor Siemens supported it but said the fear of losing low-end rentals "when there are a lot of homeless people already" is why council had held off.
status_detail: Council voiced support (minutes 9.1); no resolution was required. No measure to rehouse displaced tenants was discussed.
figures: Fines up to $1,000 per day (Mayor Funk restating staff, 0:17:25).

title: Main Street encampment: council asks staff how other cities handle encampments; mayor wants a written policy
summary: About 12 people camped at the fire-damaged former business at 447 Main St and behind a car dealership from August 2024. Councillor Jake Hiebert, who visited the camps daily, said people wanted long-term housing, jobs and addiction and mental-health help rather than food drop-offs or a cold-night shelter. Councillor Zwaagstra called encampments unacceptable; the City Manager said the owner served trespass notices and all had left by Sept 16. By consensus council asked administration to report on how other municipalities handle homelessness and encampments; the mayor asked for a written policy.
status_detail: No report or encampment policy appeared at any later recorded council meeting through Nov 3, 2026 (it may have gone to the unrecorded Strategic Priorities Committee). The City Manager confirmed there was no council-approved policy.
figures: About 12 people at the sites, 4 left by Sept 14 (J. Hiebert 0:00:08); camp first noticed in August, trespass notice Sept 5, vacated by Sept 16 (Warkentin 0:37:15).
reasons: not-council-role: a community-based issue, not a City of Steinbach issue; the city lacks expertise (Troy Warkentin); not-council-role: council's job is infrastructure, by-laws and zoning; how many tax dollars for social issues? (Jac Siemens); partners-do-it: donate to SCO, Helping Hands, Soups On; staff "are not going to solve this problem" (Michael Zwaagstra); partners-do-it: people should be helped by organizations that understand their needs (Earl Funk); enforcement-first: encampments are unacceptable; look at by-law tools other cities use (Michael Zwaagstra); provincial-responsibility: needs long-term publicly funded drug treatment and mental-health care, which Steinbach lacks (Jake Hiebert)
public: Residents and businesses complained to councillors about safety (Zwaagstra). The 14-church letter to council in 2024 cited in the existing report did not appear in any recorded meeting or minutes found.
notes: Question period item; no resolution. Minutes 18-18.2 confirm the request for a report.

title: Council declines to apply for federal Emergency Treatment Fund money for SCO's mobile outreach unit
summary: SCO asked the city to apply to the federal Emergency Treatment Fund (only municipalities could apply) and pass funds to SCO for a 16-month mobile outreach program: an addictions-trained (preferably Indigenous) worker, a vehicle, naloxone and harm-reduction supplies, and referrals to detox and rehab for people who are homeless. The City Manager's memo offered three options and noted such services are "generally outside the scope" of a municipality's obligations. Council resolved to take no action.
status_detail: R24-215 "take no action". Council did not choose the option of keeping the request open for a future intake. Application deadline was Nov 8, 2024.
figures: SCO draft budget $142,208.34: salaries $57,708.34, honorariums $5,000, vehicle $40,000, harm reduction $20,000 (package pp. 72-76); project Dec 1, 2024 - Mar 31, 2026; SCO says 30% of its clients are Indigenous and 1 detox bed serves all of Southern Health (package).
reasons: not-council-role: health and social programming is "generally outside the scope of its legislated obligations as a municipality"; city would carry program responsibility (Troy Warkentin (memo))
public: Steinbach Community Outreach (proposal by its office manager, C.K.).
seconder: unclear: minutes say 'Councillor B. Siemens' (Bill Hiebert or Jac Siemens)
notes: No transcript exists for Nov 5, 2024 (video not in the transcribed set), so any debate and members' spoken reasons are unknown. Details are from the agenda package (City Manager memo Oct 28, 2024; SCO email and proposal Oct 23, 2024) and minutes R24-215. 'Against' stance here means against applying for the fund.

title: Council directs that emergency shelters become a conditional use, prompted by The INN
summary: In approving the draft Official Community Plan and Zoning By-law changes, council added a definition of "emergency residential shelter" and made it a conditional use (public hearing required) instead of a permitted social-service use. Councillor Susan Penner said the need was recognized when The INN announced an overnight homeless shelter on Main Street.
status_detail: Carried into Zoning By-law 2245 (first/second reading Apr 1, 2025; third reading Jan 20, 2026).
reasons: neighbours-object: gives those most affected a formal way to voice concerns; applicant must have a firm plan (Susan Penner); neighbours-object: smaller areas within a zone may not suit a shelter nearby (Damian Penner); neighbours-object: a 24-hour shelter has a different impact than a daytime social service (Michael Zwaagstra)
public: No public input at this meeting; public engagement was scheduled for January 2025.
vote: unanimous (Mayor Funk and Councillor Jake Hiebert absent; Deputy Mayor Zwaagstra chaired)

title: Adult & Teen Challenge's thrift store and addictions office denied a site in the industrial park
summary: Adult & Teen Challenge, a residential addiction-recovery program, had to leave 354 Main St and asked to run its thrift store (work therapy) with counselling offices at 86 Industrial Road, which needed conditional use for retail in the M1 zone. Council denied it unanimously to protect industrial land, while praising the organization.
status_detail: Denied (R25-034). Whether the program found another site is not recorded at council.
figures: About 2,500 sq ft of its 7,000 sq ft on Main Street used for support groups and daily addiction counselling (delegate, 0:31:00).
reasons: wrong-location: conditional use runs with the land; taxpayer-built industrial parks should not become retail (Jac Siemens); wrong-location: protect the integrity of the industrial park (Michael Zwaagstra)
public: Applicant S.H. (Avedo Inc.) and D.E. (Adult & Teen Challenge) spoke for it; the program faced a deadline to move before winter.
notes: Included because it concerns a local addictions-recovery provider; the decision itself was a land-use one.

title: Asked if council has a homelessness strategy, the mayor says it is not municipal jurisdiction
summary: At the zoning hearing a member of the public asked whether council has a homelessness strategy. Mayor Funk said he was working on things with the provincial minister but a homeless strategy "doesn't fall under municipal jurisdiction," and that other governments download responsibilities onto the city. He had made the same downloading point about affordable housing two weeks earlier.
status_detail: No city homelessness strategy was adopted through Nov 2026. The CSWB plan (Mar 2026) is a community plan, not a city strategy. The mayor and Councillor Susan Penner met the provincial Housing Minister on Jun 30, 2026 (SteinbachOnline, per existing report; not discussed at a recorded meeting).
reasons: not-council-role: a direct homeless strategy does not fall under municipal jurisdiction; city handles land use, sewer, water, roads (Earl Funk); provincial-responsibility: other governments download responsibilities; housing is "usually in their basket" (Earl Funk)
public: N.P. (St. Malo) asked the question and what happens if transitional housing fits no category.
notes: "Minister Smith" presumably Manitoba's minister responsible for housing/homelessness (Bernadette Smith); not confirmed in the transcript.

title: Zoning By-law 2245 adopted with emergency shelters as a conditional use, against the consultant's advice
summary: At the April 1, 2025 hearing most speakers came about the shelter change. The city's planning consultant (WSP) confirmed it had recommended keeping emergency shelters a permitted use. The INN's board said it was now a transitional-housing project, opposed the by-law, and warned that being classed as an emergency shelter would cost over $600,000 in government funding. Staff said transitional housing was not defined in the by-law. Council gave first and second readings unanimously; objections sent the by-law to the Manitoba Municipal Board, which ordered no changes, and third reading passed Jan 20, 2026.
status_detail: By-law 2245 in force from Jan 20, 2026 (R26-015). The gap for transitional housing was filled later by By-law 2275 (June 2026), also as a conditional use.
figures: Over $600,000 in potential funding at risk (L.D., The INN, 1:23:50); The Carillon reported 49 written objections and 10 letters of support (existing report; minutes say only "several items of correspondence"). By-law shortened from 155 to 106 pages (Zwaagstra 2:00:15).
reasons: neighbours-object: neighbourhoods should have a formal mechanism; same rules as any residential use in a commercial zone (Susan Penner); neighbours-object: many people came to councillors; a hearing lets everyone be heard (Earl Funk); neighbours-object: community should be able to comment on a specific shelter plan (Damian Penner); neighbours-object: like funeral homes or hospitals, it may or may not fit a location (medium-confidence ID) (Michael Zwaagstra); study-first: no detailed plan from The INN before council; staff need a site plan to classify it (Earl Funk)
public: L.D. (The INN board) opposed: the INN bought 447 Main St because shelters were permitted, was not included in early discussions, and is transitional housing with case management, not an emergency shelter. L.C. objected that conditional use leaves room for discrimination and cited a human-rights case against a Manitoba municipality (her legal characterization; unverified). T.C. asked how applicants are protected from discrimination; N.P. asked whether council has a homelessness strategy; T.B. objected to more zoning division. B.U. (a neighbour and former INN board member) and K.U. supported the conditional use, citing neighbourhood safety; B.B. supported it as a healthy community process.
mover: Susan Penner (1st); Jac Siemens (2nd); Michael Zwaagstra (3rd)
seconder: Damian Penner (1st); Jake Hiebert (2nd); Jake Hiebert (3rd)
notes: Count of written objections/supports not confirmed from the minutes or package. The INN board speaker's name appears in the minutes; initials used here.

title: Private overnight security patrols hired and continued into 2026
summary: Citing RCMP shortages and property crime, council hired a private security firm (pilot from Jul 2, 2025) funded from unspent RCMP budget, then continued nightly 10 pm - 6 am patrols to year-end and put $145,000 in the 2026 budget for consideration. Homelessness was not mentioned in either debate; included as context for the city's enforcement capacity.
status_detail: R25-118 (Jun 17, 2025) and R25-209 (Nov 4, 2025), both unanimous.
figures: $145,000 estimated for 2026; patrols 7 days a week, 10 to 6 (Thiessen, Nov 4 2025, 0:04:32 and 0:07:27).
notes: Not a homelessness decision; kept for context (existing report Finding 5).

title: Transitional housing added to the zoning by-law, but as a conditional use, not permitted as The INN asked
summary: An application on behalf of The INN asked council to define transitional housing and make it a permitted use in the C-2 zone. Administration recommended a broader definition and a conditional use in seven zones. Council adopted that version: first reading Apr 21, 2026, and second and third readings Jun 2, 2026 after a hearing at which no one spoke and no letters were received.
status_detail: By-law 2275 in force: transitional housing now has a category (conditional in RMD, RHD, RMX, C1, C2, C3, CMX; 1 parking space per 5 units or beds). No site-specific conditional-use hearing for The INN at 447 Main St appeared on a council agenda through Nov 3, 2026.
figures: Occupancy typically 3 months to 3 years (definition, Warkentin 0:42:52); parking 1 space per 5 units/beds (Warkentin 0:45:53).
reasons: neighbours-object: neighbourhoods must weigh in on projects that may change their nature (Susan Penner); neighbours-object: could change the character of a neighbourhood; would not support a permitted use (Michael Zwaagstra); neighbours-object: consistency: any multifamily or co-living use is conditional; neighbourhood voice (Earl Funk); neighbours-object: hearings let the community and council have input (Jac Siemens)
public: Applicant L.C. on behalf of The INN (application); no one spoke at the Jun 2 hearing and no written correspondence was received.
mover: Susan Penner (1st); Michael Zwaagstra (2nd); Jac Siemens (3rd)
seconder: Michael Zwaagstra (1st); Damian Penner (2nd); Jake Hiebert (3rd)
notes: The transcript renders "The INN" as "VNN" at 0:43:46 (Apr 21). Status after Nov 3, 2026 of The INN's permit is unknown (Feb 2026 assisted-living refusal was reported by The Carillon, not at a recorded meeting).

title: Council endorses SCO and Eden's supportive housing project, The Bridge on Third
summary: Steinbach Community Outreach and Eden Healthcare Services asked for a formal endorsement to include with grant applications. Council passed a resolution of support; members cited The Bridge's success and a growing homeless population. The endorsement carries no city money, land or fee waivers.
status_detail: Endorsement letter approved (R26-096). Funding of the project depends on the province and others.
figures: 30 supportive units (SteinbachOnline, per existing report; not stated at the meeting).
public: Letter from L.K. on behalf of the project; the organizations had presented to an (unrecorded) committee meeting.
notes: An unidentified councillor (speaker F, low confidence) also spoke in support at 0:20:41.

title: Councillor Siemens reports homelessness as a national theme at FCM
summary: In his opening, Councillor Siemens reported that chronic homelessness, mental health and addiction were key topics at the 2026 FCM conference, asking how Steinbach should respond.
status_detail: Opening remarks; no follow-up motion.

title: Residents' letter about unhoused people near Loewen Blvd and Oak Crescent: safety officers respond
summary: Residents C.F. and A.F. wrote about people frequenting the transit shelter at Loewen Blvd and Henry St and the Oak Crescent-Henry St pathway. The City Manager reported that community safety officers had already checked the area, talked with the unhoused people there, encouraged them to use social-service agencies, and found no hazards; council took the letter as information.
status_detail: Received as information after the CSO check; no further action or policy.
reasons: partners-do-it: officers refer unhoused people to social service organizations (Troy Warkentin)
public: Letter from residents C.F. and A.F. (contents not in the public package available).
notes: This is the "Oak Crescent" item; no encampment removal was reported.

title: $200,000 provincial safety grant: homelessness eligible, staff propose a truck and cameras; decision deferred
summary: The city received an unexpected $200,000 provincial public-safety grant to be spent by Mar 31, 2027. Staff listed CSWB priorities including "affordable housing and homelessness" as eligible, but recommended $65,000 for a second community-safety-officer truck and $135,000 for security cameras. Councillors questioned why the library was left out and raised privacy concerns, and the item was deferred to an August meeting.
status_detail: No decision found in the Aug 4 transcript or the Aug 4 and Aug 18 minutes, or later recorded meetings through Nov 3, 2026. No council member proposed using it for homelessness.
figures: $200,000; $65,000 CSO truck + $135,000 cameras recommended; spend by Mar 31, 2027 (Thiessen 1:22:18; minutes).
notes: Speaker S at 1:22:16 ("Yes, thank you.") is a mislabel; the presentation is O = Adam Thiessen.

title: RCMP report: Mental Health Act calls up from 251 to 311 year-to-date
summary: The RCMP detachment commander told council that Mental Health Act calls rose from 251 (2025 to date) to 311 (2026 to date), more than one a day, with police spending much time with partner agencies on mental-health crises.
status_detail: Report received; no council action on mental-health capacity recorded.
